title: Fast & Slow Pointers
tagline: Two runners at different speeds detect cycles, find midpoints, and locate cycle starts in O(1) space.

intuition.analogy: On a circular running track, a fast runner doing two laps for every one of a slow runner will eventually lap and meet the slow runner. On a straight track with a finish line, the fast runner simply reaches the end first. Whether they ever meet tells you if the track loops.
paragraphs: Linked lists hide their shape — you can't index into them, and a corrupted 'next' pointer can create a cycle. Floyd's tortoise-and-hare uses two pointers, one moving one node per step and one moving two, to probe that shape using only constant memory.

If the list is straight, the fast pointer hits null and you know there's no cycle. If there's a loop, the fast pointer keeps circling and the gap to the slow pointer shrinks by one each step, so they're guaranteed to collide inside the loop.
The same speed trick finds the middle of a list in one pass (when fast reaches the end, slow is at the midpoint) and, with a clever second phase, pinpoints exactly where a cycle begins.
intuition.keyIdea: Relative speed forces a meeting inside any cycle; reaching null proves there is none — all in O(1) space.

steps.title: Advance at two speeds
steps.detail: slow = slow.next (one step); fast = fast.next.next (two steps), guarding against fast or fast.next being null.

steps.title: Detect
steps.detail: If fast (or fast.next) becomes null, there's no cycle. If slow == fast, they've met inside a cycle.

steps.title: Find the cycle start (optional)
steps.detail: After a meeting, reset one pointer to the head and advance both by one step; they meet again exactly at the cycle's entry node (a consequence of the distance math).

code.title: detect_cycle.py

complexity.timeReason: The slow pointer travels at most the list length before a meeting or termination.
complexity.spaceReason: Two pointers — no hash set of visited nodes required.

pitfalls: Null checks: test both fast and fast.next before the double hop, or you'll dereference null.
Initialise both at head; starting fast one ahead changes the midpoint result for even-length lists.
The cycle-start phase only works after a confirmed meeting, not before.

rows: fast wrapped past the loop start
dryRun.clickMoment: Once both pointers are inside the loop, the fast pointer closes the gap by exactly one node per step. A shrinking integer gap must hit zero — so a meeting is inevitable.

problems.title: Linked List Cycle
problems.statement: Detect whether a linked list has a cycle.
problems.hint: Tortoise and hare; meeting means a cycle.

problems.title: Linked List Cycle II
problems.statement: Return the node where the cycle begins, or null.
problems.hint: After meeting, move one pointer to head; advance both by one until they meet again.

problems.title: Middle of the Linked List
problems.statement: Return the middle node of a linked list.
problems.hint: When fast reaches the end, slow is at the middle.

problems.title: Happy Number
problems.statement: Detect if repeatedly summing squared digits reaches 1.
problems.hint: The sequence is a 'linked list' of numbers; use fast/slow to detect the loop.

problems.title: Find the Duplicate Number
problems.statement: Find the duplicate in n+1 numbers from 1..n without modifying the array.
problems.hint: Treat values as next-pointers; the duplicate creates a cycle whose entrance is the answer.
problems.tests: Cycle-start trick on an array as a function graph.
